City Council Approves Major Transit Overhaul After Months of Debate

By Lena Morales

RIVERTON — In a decisive 7–2 vote on Tuesday night, the Riverton City Council approved a comprehensive overhaul of the city’s public transit system aimed at reducing congestion and improving service reliability across all neighborhoods. The new plan, which will take effect in phases beginning next spring, reallocates funding to expand bus routes, increase frequency during peak hours, and upgrade several key transit hubs.

Council members cited months of public meetings, feedback from daily commuters, and independent studies that identified persistent delays and overcrowding on main corridors. “This plan responds directly to the concerns residents raised,” said Council President Maria Chen. “We focused on realistic, phased improvements that will make daily travel easier for thousands of people.”

The approved measures include the addition of four new express routes, dedicated bus lanes on two of the city’s busiest avenues, and a pilot program to extend weekend service in underserved districts. Officials estimate the changes will cut average commute times by 12 to 18 percent for riders on impacted routes.

Community leaders welcomed the decision but urged continued engagement as implementation begins. “This is a strong step forward, but execution matters,” said Jamal Ortiz, director of the East Riverton Neighborhood Association. “We need transparent updates and opportunities for riders to report issues once the new routes start.”

Funding for the project will come from a combination of reallocated municipal transportation funds, a state grant awarded earlier this year, and a modest increase in the city’s transportation levy that voters approved in last year’s ballot. City staff also plan to seek federal matching funds for infrastructure upgrades.

Transportation Director Priya Singh outlined a phased timeline that prioritizes high-impact changes in the first year, including the new express routes and improvements to bus stops and real-time arrival signage. Later phases will focus on lane reconfigurations and hub renovations that require more extensive construction.

The city plans to launch an online portal and a mobile app feature where riders can track route changes, service alerts, and offer feedback. Officials say they will hold monthly town halls during the rollout to keep the public informed.

Mayor Daniel Brooks praised the council for what he called a “measured and community-centered approach.” He said his office will work closely with transit agencies to monitor performance and make adjustments as needed.

Opponents of the plan voiced concerns about potential impacts on car traffic and parking in corridor neighborhoods. Two council members voted against the measure, asserting that more traffic studies were needed. Supporters countered that the long-term benefits of shifting commuters to reliable transit would outweigh temporary disruptions during construction.

City staff will present a progress report to the council six months after initial implementation, and a full evaluation will be conducted after 18 months to assess ridership changes, on-time performance, and community feedback.

Residents with questions or who wish to provide input can find details and the project timeline on the city’s transportation department website or attend the next public forum scheduled for April 10 at the Civic Center.
